title: Why Chicago Became a Gospel Center

grade_definitions.VERIFIED: Confirmed by primary, archival, or government evidence, or by direct institutional records; contradiction absent.
grade_definitions.SUPPORTED: Backed by reputable secondary, scholarly, or institutional sources; stronger (primary) confirmation still desirable.
grade_definitions.PROVISIONAL: Plausible working interpretation with partial evidence; stated as hypothesis.
grade_definitions.UNRESOLVED: Claimed but not evidenced in this pass; do not repeat as fact.

claims.claim: Chicago gospel developed incrementally from the 1920s — beginning in Pentecostal/Holiness churches and spreading into mainline Protestant churches in the 1930s — rather than through a single founding moment.
claims.date_of_evidence: 2016 (review of Marovich, A City Called Heaven)
claims.evidence: Braxton Shelley's peer-reviewed assessment states Marovich rejects an instantaneous 'big bang': gospel developed incrementally from the 1920s, first in Pentecostal/Holiness churches, then into mainline Protestant churches in the 1930s.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None on the incremental framing; the 'big bang' myth persists in popular and promotional accounts.
claims.notes: Adopted as the brief's central analytical frame: Chicago was a networked center, not a single-place invention.

claims.claim: The Great Migration brought large numbers of southern Black migrants to Chicago, creating the audience, church demand, and musical mixing that gospel needed.
claims.evidence: LOC records the Staple Singers relocating to Chicago as part of the Great Migration and scoring a 1956 Vee-Jay gospel hit; PBS's GOSPEL series frames Black gospel soaring 'to new heights during the Great Migration'; WTTW traces Dorsey's arrival during the Migration.
claims.notes: Standard historical context; treated as a conditioning factor, not a monocausal explanation.

claims.claim: At Ebenezer Missionary Baptist Church, Rev. James Smith called for a gospel chorus on December 6, 1931; Theodore Frye directed it with Thomas A. Dorsey at the piano; the roughly 100-member chorus debuted in January 1932.
claims.evidence: Chicago Patterns reproduces a Vivian G. Harsh Research Collection quotation describing Smith's December 6, 1931 call, Frye directing, Dorsey at piano, and the January 1932 debut of the ~100-member chorus.
claims.notes: Reached via secondary reproduction; direct inspection of the Harsh Collection is outstanding. Do not upgrade to VERIFIED until then.

claims.claim: Ebenezer Missionary Baptist Church is the home of the first modern gospel choir.
claims.date_of_evidence: n.d. (institutional self-statement); 1931–32 events; 2013 (Congressional Record on Pilgrim)
claims.evidence: Ebenezer's own site claims it; the 1931–32 chorus episode is documented (CL03); but Pilgrim Baptist has a competing, institutionally recognized gospel-choir origin (Congressional Record: Dorsey organizing a gospel chorus there at Pastor Austin's request in 1931/32).
claims.contradictory_evidence: Pilgrim's documented chorus organization (S05); the sibling audit explicitly identifies competing Pilgrim-vs-Ebenezer 'birthplace' claims and recommends attributing both rather than choosing a winner.
claims.notes: Outcome turns on the definition of 'gospel choir.' Report both claims with attribution; do not declare a winner.

claims.claim: Pilgrim Baptist Church purchased the former Kehilath Anshe Ma'ariv synagogue at 3301 S. Indiana Ave. in 1922; Thomas A. Dorsey joined in 1931 at Pastor Junius C. Austin's request to organize a gospel chorus.
claims.evidence: Congressional Record states the 1922 purchase and Dorsey's 1931 arrival at Austin's request to organize a gospel chorus. The 1981 city landmark report independently confirms the 3301 S. Indiana address and that the Pilgrim congregation has been housed there since 1922.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Other reputable accounts (New Georgia Encyclopedia via sibling) date Dorsey's music-director start to 1932 rather than 1931 — consistent if 1931 marks arrival/chorus organizing and 1932 the formal directorship.
claims.notes: S05 is a legislative tribute (Extensions of Remarks), not a primary congregational record — hence SUPPORTED, not VERIFIED.

claims.claim: Dorsey served as Pilgrim's music director from the early 1930s into the late 1970s — roughly five decades.
claims.evidence: Multiple accounts place his tenure from 1932 into the late 1970s; NMAAHC's object record describes him as Pilgrim's music director hired by Pastor Austin 'in the 1930s' and notes the church 'became known as the birthplace of gospel music' under him.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Exact tenure length varies across accounts ('50,' '55,' '60 years,' or 'into the late 1970s'). Start year 1931 vs 1932 also varies (see CL05).
claims.notes: Use the bounded formulation 'from the early 1930s into the late 1970s' unless primary congregational records settle it.

claims.claim: The National Convention of Gospel Choirs and Choruses (NCGCC) was founded by Dorsey (with associates) in 1933.
claims.evidence: Word in Black/NNPA reports a 1932 founding; NCGCC-derived promotional copy states 1933; Harris documents a pivotal 1932 convocation involving Ebenezer, Pilgrim, and Metropolitan's W. D. Cook choir; JHU describes Sallie Martin's role in the NCGCC's 1933 launch.
claims.notes: PROVISIONAL reconciliation: 1932 may mark the precursor convocation and 1933 the formal organization. Grade remains DISPUTED until primary organizational records (minutes, incorporation, programs) settle it.

claims.claim: Roberta Martin's first church position was pianist for Ebenezer's Young People's Choir; Dorsey and Theodore Frye guided her early career; she organized the Martin-Frye Quartet in 1933, which became the Roberta Martin Singers in 1936, with women joining in the mid-1940s.
claims.evidence: Smithsonian archival description of the Roberta Martin Singers records states her Ebenezer Young People's Choir post, Dorsey/Frye guidance, the 1933 Martin-Frye Quartet, its 1936 renaming, and women joining mid-1940s; calls her an important 1930s gospel pioneer.
claims.notes: Demonstrates the ensemble/training pipeline: church choir -> small group -> touring ensemble -> mixed-gender group.

claims.claim: Sallie Martin introduced Dorsey's music in Chicago-area Black churches, managed finances and developed markets, and helped launch the Dorsey House of Music (1932) and the NCGCC (1933).
claims.evidence: JHU library description states Martin introduced Dorsey's music in Chicago-area Black churches, handled finances and market development, and helped launch the Dorsey House of Music in 1932 and the NCGCC in 1933.
claims.notes: Positions a Black woman as the business/distribution engine of early gospel — counters the composer-genius-only narrative.

claims.claim: Kenneth Morris arranged and transcribed songs at Bowles' House of Music; Rev. Clarence H. Cobbs installed him at First Church of Deliverance and provided financial help to launch the Martin & Morris Music Company (1940), which carried hundreds of songs and distributed them nationally.
claims.evidence: CPL's Martin and Morris papers finding aid: Morris arranged/transcribed at Bowles' House of Music; Cobbs installed Morris at First Church of Deliverance; Cobbs provided financial help to launch the company; the company distributed songs nationally. JHU: its books carried hundreds of songs from established and emerging composers.
claims.notes: Publishing as network infrastructure, not mere authorship. Note Bowles' House of Music as a pre-existing node — an avenue for follow-up research.

claims.claim: First Church of Deliverance, under Rev. Clarence H. Cobbs, launched a radio broadcast in 1935 and acquired an early Hammond organ in 1939 on Kenneth Morris's recommendation; the broadcast exposed listeners to the new sound, drew audiences to the church, and the Hammond sound spread among churches.
claims.evidence: NPR Illinois reports Cobbs's 1935 broadcast, the 1939 Hammond acquisition on Morris's recommendation, the broadcast's role in exposing listeners and drawing audiences, and the sound's spread among churches.
claims.notes: A clean infrastructure chain: person (Morris) -> technology (Hammond) -> institution (church) -> medium (radio) -> diffusion. Radio-station call letters not verified in this pass — research next.

claims.claim: Vee-Jay Records maintained a substantial gospel catalog (Staple Singers, Caravans, Swan Silvertones); the Staple Singers' 'Uncloudy Day' was a 1956 Vee-Jay gospel hit, and the group relocated to Chicago as part of the Great Migration.
claims.evidence: LOC National Recording Registry essay states the 1956 Vee-Jay gospel hit 'Uncloudy Day' and the Staple Singers' Chicago relocation as part of the Great Migration.
claims.notes: Use Vee-Jay as a later expansion/distribution node, not as an origin institution.

claims.claim: Mahalia Jackson migrated to Chicago in 1927, found work as a domestic, and credited Chicago's organizational and business environment with opening possibilities for her.
claims.evidence: Jackson's autobiography (reproduced in the ASHP/CUNY teaching resource): she migrated to Chicago in 1927, worked as a domestic, joined gospel activity, and credited Chicago's organizational/business environment.
claims.notes: Firsthand but retrospective (1966, recalling 1927). Corroboration from contemporary 1920s records not attempted in this pass.

claims.claim: A fire on January 6, 2006 gutted Pilgrim Baptist Church, destroying decades of records and likely/reportably original Dorsey sheet music.
claims.evidence: RNS (Jan. 12, 2006): the fire gutted the building; possible original sheet music had not yet been inventoried and might have been destroyed. Later reporting (GRAMMY.com) states photographs and Dorsey sheet music were gone.
claims.contradictory_evidence: The contemporary RNS wording is cautious ('might have been destroyed'); later accounts are firmer. Item-level loss documentation was not found in this pass.
claims.notes: Best wording: the fire destroyed decades of records and 'likely or reportedly' destroyed original Dorsey sheet music — do not claim every item's loss is documented. Major evidentiary loss shaping this brief's limits.

claims.claim: Mahalia Jackson made her paid debut at Pilgrim Baptist Church in 1928 for $4.
claims.evidence: Inherited from sibling CTL-DR-MUSIC-001; its own audit notes the claim rests on a weak Tribune/WYND retrospective.
claims.notes: Do NOT repeat as fact. Requires a primary or strong contemporary source. Flagged for follow-up research.

claims.claim: Carl Van Vechten's portrait of Mahalia Jackson (April 16, 1962; LOC repro. no. LC-USZ62-91314) is public domain per LOC's rights statement, with a credit requirement.
claims.evidence: LOC's Carl Van Vechten Collection rights statement: 'no known copyright restrictions'; restrictions on use expired 1986; credit the photographer; do not crop or colorize. Van Vechten died 1964.
claims.contradictory_evidence: LOC warns privacy/publicity rights may apply — reviewed: subject (Jackson, d. Jan. 27, 1972) falls outside the stated 50-year Illinois post-mortem period (elapsed Jan. 27, 2022). Recorded, not relied on as legal advice.
claims.notes: Selected as sourced visual V2 (see visuals.md).

claims.claim: The piano held by NMAAHC (object 2015.134.1a-g) is the 1930s Conover baby grand used by Thomas A. Dorsey as a rehearsal piano at Pilgrim Baptist Church; rights: 'No Known Copyright Restrictions.'
claims.evidence: NMAAHC object record: 'This piano once resided in the historical Pilgrim Baptist Church of Chicago, Illinois, where it was used as a rehearsal piano by music director, Thomas A. Dorsey'; made by The Cable Piano Company (Conover), 1930s; gift of the Keller family; Restrictions & Rights: 'No Known Copyright Restrictions.'
claims.notes: Selected as sourced visual V1 (see visuals.md). Also supplies institutional context: Dorsey hired by Pastor Austin 'in the 1930s'; Pilgrim 'became known as the birthplace of gospel music'; Albertina Walker, Mahalia Jackson, Sallie Martin, Aretha Franklin, James Cleveland, the Staple Singers, and the Edwin Hawkins Singers sang there; Bessie Coleman was a congregant.

claims.claim: Thomas A. Dorsey wrote his first gospel song in 1921.
claims.evidence: Sibling CTL-DR-MUSIC-001 asserts 1921 ('If You See My Savior' era). Harris's scholarship (S11) documents Dorsey's 'If You See My Savior' circulating by 1930; Dorsey worked as secular bluesman 'Georgia Tom' through the 1920s.
claims.contradictory_evidence: The 1921 date conflicts with the documented 1920s blues career and with 1929–1932 as the conventional dating of his gospel turn. No primary manuscript or dated publication found in this pass.
claims.notes: Do not use 1921 as a settled date. The gospel turn is best described as a process across 1928–1932.

claims.claim: Standard reference dates for Mahalia Jackson: born October 26, 1911, New Orleans; died January 27, 1972.
claims.evidence: None gathered in this pass.
claims.notes: Widely repeated in reference works but NOT independently verified here. Used only the death date as a boundary for the publicity-rights review (CL16). Verify before any CTL publication that depends on it.

claims.claim: Chicago gospel's infrastructure combined: storefront/Holiness practice, established churches (Ebenezer, Pilgrim, Metropolitan), sheet-music publishing (Dorsey House of Music; Martin & Morris), a national convention (NCGCC), radio (First Church of Deliverance, 1935), new instrument technology (Hammond, 1939), touring ensembles (Roberta Martin Singers; Caravans), and record labels (Vee-Jay).
claims.evidence: Synthesis of the ledger's individually supported claims: incremental development across church types (S01); publishing houses (S12, S13); radio + Hammond (S14); Vee-Jay distribution (S15); ensemble/training pipeline (S03); national convention (S09).
claims.notes: This is the brief's thesis claim. Each component carries its own grade; the synthesis is SUPPORTED, not VERIFIED, because it is an interpretive integration.

graph_rules_applied.note: Per CTL graph rules: only VERIFIED claims feed graph ingestion as verified edges. SUPPORTED claims may appear with their grade visible. Sibling-inherited claims (S29) were not silently promoted.
